newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean government challenges unions to TV debate.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean government challenges unions to TV debate.

text.p: South Korea's ruling party chief on Saturday challenged union leaders to a televised debate over a controversial new labour law in a dramatic change of tack to try to turn public opinion against strikers.
Hours after police tried to arrest militant heads of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, New Korea Party chairman Lee Hong-koo was inviting them to go on air for a live debate.
Amid other signs that the government was abandoning confrontation and seeking dialogue, Lee told reporters he would meet any union leader.

He made clear, though, the government had no intention of revising the bill that allows companies to lay off workers and hire temporary staff to break strikes, shattering a jobs-for-life labour tradition.
Confederation president Kwon Young-kil was unenthusiastic, saying the government should first scrap the law.

Public opinion is seen as a make-or-break factor in the stoppages that have closed car plants and disrupted hospitals. Unions have threatened the biggest strike in the nation's history next Tuesday and Wednesday.
Official figures released on Saturday show production losses due to strikes have mounted to $2 billion and export losses are at $345 million.
Unions denounce the legislation as an "evil law", and international labour organisations have said it is even harsher than the law it replaced.
Bu officials dismiss domestic and international hostility as a "misunderstanding". They say the law is needed to rescue the economy from a worrying downturn.
"I've spoken to labour officials and there have been a lot of misunderstandings," a party spokesman quoted Lee as telling local reporters.
"That's why we proposed discussing the issue openly through a television debate."
Asked if he would personally join the studio debate, Lee said: "If I could help, I will appear on television."

"Chairman Lee said the party does not want to resolve everything by mobilising official forces. He said the party wanted to resolve the matter in a reasonable way through dialogue," the spokesman said.

Earlier on Saturday, workers wielding iron pipes chased away police trying to issue arrest warrants on seven leaders of the confederation camped on the icy grounds of Seoul's Roman Catholic Myongdong Cathedral.
However, a prosecution source said state prosecutors wanted to avoid violence and were negotiating with church officials to find a way to serve the warrants peacefully.
Yonhap Television News quoted an unidentified government official as saying arrest warrants would not be served without the church's agreement.

Many South Koreans are ambivalent about the new law, recognising that South Korea's labour market must be made more flexible to improve industrial competitiveness yet worried it could spark mass redundancies.
But there is public anger at the way the law was rammed through parliament in a six-minute dawn session attended only by New Korea Party deputies.
Confederation president Kwon and six deputies are camped out in Myondong a makeshift plastic tent pitched beneath a statue of the Virgin Mary.
On Saturday they too appeared to back away from violent confrontation, shaken by an attempted suicide by a Hyundai car worker on Friday who set himself on fire.
"We will continue to stage protest rallies but will refrain from extreme actions such as suicide attempts," a confederation spokesman said.
Union leaders ordered strikers to resume "partial production" until next week's general strike.
